Question: What are the key findings from the differential geometry of curves?
Old_Answer: I'm not aware what the OP wants to know from this question. Differential geometry of curves involves the Frenet frame attached to the curve. The frame constitutes T , N , B which are orthogonal vectors attached to the curve in space and form equations called the Frenet formulas which allow us to derive mathematical measurements of the turning and twisting of a curve in say R 3 . Later on, this Frenet apparatus was generalized by Darboux to the theory of surfaces by introducing the method of moving frames. Cartan brought this moving frame method to full generality. The essential idea is simple. To each point of the object under study ( a curve, a surface, a Euclidean space itself,..) assign a frame. Then using orthonormal expansion express the rate of change of the frame in terms of the frame itself. This, of course, is just what the Frenet apparatus does in the case of a curve. The choice of the frame is very important. Later on, when connection forms come into picture, the subject gets more generalized and sophisticated. Ordinary derivative is replaced with covariant derivative. What a connection one-form tells us? Take a look at the equation. ω i j ( v ) = ∇ v E i . E j ( p ) The connection one-form ω i j is the initial rate at which E i rotates towards E j as p moves in the v direction. Connection forms form connection equations. These equations have a striking similarity to the Frenet formulas for curves. All books on differential geometry which go upto connection forms display this obvious relation between the geometry of curves and geometry of surfaces. Remember, covariant derivatives treat curved surfaces and hypersurfaces. Finally, the connection forms satisfy the famous Cartan structural equations. Everything comes under the domain of differential forms. One equation connects dual forms to connection forms. Dual forms describe the dual of the frame field. Other equation connects curvature forms to connection forms. This looks complicated and boring. But this forms the basis of the calculation of curvature of spacetime in general relativity for several types of metrics. Misner-Thorne-Wheeler's Gravitation leans heavily on connection forms and curvature forms via Cartan's equations. And all graduate level texts such as Wald's General Relativity discuss curvature in terms of connection forms besides other methods. Eventually, the approach goes to the level of Newman-Penrose null tetrad method which is something of a “dinosaur” in calculating curvature of “unfamiliar" metrics of spacetime. What starts as a simple differential geometry of a curve in space gives rise to a very heavy mathematical technology in sophisticated forms of general relativity and other related topics in theoretical physics.
